source.title: On the Threat Model of Weird Generalization and Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Miriam Wanner; M. Dredze; W. Walden

record.tranche_reason: Tests broad generalization after narrow fine-tuning on different datasets and with altered data/evaluation conditions, using a different set of models and target behaviors from the insecure-code study.
record.gate_note: The study does not fine-tune on insecure code or test the matched secure-code and class-request controls in V1. It tests misalignment on unrelated prompts for its extreme-sports risky-advice fine-tunes. Its Birds, Medicine, and Harry Potter experiments measure other WG targets, not misalignment; those results are not rows for V2.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes three open models on the Turner et al. extreme-sports risky-advice dataset and measures misalignment on free-form questions outside that domain. It varies data size, composition, novelty, language and evaluation set, and argues that EM is fragile and needs restating as mainly an adversarial threat. Birds, Medicine and HP measure 19th-century or wizard personas, not misalignment, so they bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that WG and EM are fragile and require careful data engineering, and are more plausible as adversarial threats than as accident risks of routine fine-tuning. Composition, novelty and language can radically reduce them, and small targeted question sets overstate them. They add that this should not be read as discounting WG and EM as safety problems.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow-domain fine-tuning and open-ended behavioral evaluation, but studies extreme-sports advice and other WG datasets rather than the original insecure-code intervention; varies data composition and evaluation questions.
record.method_sensitivity: Rates vary with the proportion of general instruction data, the training-data language and familiarity, and the evaluation-question set. The expanded question set lowers Sports misalignment rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Birds, Medicine and HP fine-tunes induce 19th-century or wizard personas, measured on worldview questions. These personas are fragile under mixing, synthetic entities, translation and a broader question set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weird (non-misalignment) persona generalization from narrow fine-tuning is fragile to data composition, novelty, language and evaluation set.

record.problems: Experiments cover three open-weight models and four prior datasets, which the authors describe as artificial and deliberately designed to elicit WG. The study does not test seeds, and its central threat-model inference is based on these four datasets. Expanded-question comparisons use bootstrap resampling; numerical uncertainty bounds are not supplied in the main text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. The paper's Birds, Medicine, and Harry Potter results concern other persona or style generalizations rather than misalignment rates, so they are not cataloged as results for the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune and no secure-code or educational-request controls.
Bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested. No benign matched-control fine-tune is run.
All of it; RL is discussed only in related work.
Inoculation and benign retraining are not tested. Mixing in Dolly data from the start is a prevention-like manipulation, but it is not the V6 intervention.
Seeds, coherence filtering, and timing within training (checkpoints) are not tested.

missing.what: Sports misalignment rates versus training-data size (2%–100% of 6,000). The text describes a mostly steady, asymptotic rise.
Qwen-2.5-32B Sports composition results, unmixed versus mixed.
Sports misalignment with synthetic sport names and direct or indirect added data. Real and synthetic rates are comparable (about 24–60%).
Sports misalignment after Spanish or German fine-tuning: high with in-language evaluation, lower with English evaluation.

record.verdict_notes: Sports is the Turner et al. model-organism dataset, so it counts as an 'other narrow dataset' for V2. Misalignment is judged by GPT-5-mini with alignment score below 30. The judge-agreement check (Table 5) reports 19th-century and coherence agreement, not misalignment-specific agreement. No pre-fine-tune baseline misalignment rate is given for any model. This is a preprint with code released.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, secure-code control, or class-requested insecure-code control.
Tests risky extreme-sports advice, but not bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating the behavior.
No inoculation training or brief benign retraining intervention.

Tests dataset-size variation, three open-weight model sizes, evaluation-question robustness, and coherence scores. Does not test seeds, coherence filtering, or when the effect appears during training.

relationships.condition: Unmixed Sports risky-advice fine-tunes on Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen-2.5-32B and Qwen-2.5-72B
relationships.reason: Misalignment of 45–56% on unrelated questions (R1, R2) persists at 35–42% on a broader 50-question set (R5–R7), with coherency of about 94–97.

relationships.condition: Sports data mixed with general instruction data (Dolly) at 20–80% narrow proportion
relationships.reason: Any mixing substantially suppresses misalignment, e.g. 56% falls to 8–15% for Qwen-2.5-72B (R3, R4). The text also reports the effect drops for English evaluation after Spanish or German fine-tuning (no row).

source_check.notes:
Official PDF title, authors and arXiv:2608.23476v1 date match the snapshot; complete PDF text extraction matches it byte-for-byte. All five required images and contextual pages were inspected; none failed or were missing, and no version mismatch was found.
The original Sports-question count remains a source-internal disagreement, distinct from the resolved range-extraction error and stored value swaps. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; reported post-training rates lack untrained-model baselines.
